threads.subject: (Non)-accompanying dependents / proof of citizenship-REP-2017-1800
threads.question:
From ### Good morning,
Amongst fellow RCICs we have been discussing how to proceed on a spousal sponsorship when there is a child who may be eligible for Canadian citizenship.
Specifically:
1. Is the child eligible for urgent processing of their Proof of Citizenship application due to the concurrent spousal sponsorship of their parent?
2. Once we've filed their Proof of Citizenship application and included that proof in the Spousal Sponsorship application, how do we indicate on the IMM0008 and otherwise that the child will be accompanying if they AREN'T deemed a citizen? Ie. should they be declared as non-accompanying or accompanying, and when?
3. Since the process ing for Proof of Citizenship is currently much longer than Spousal Sponsorship, does this cause a delay in processing? Ie. will the Spousal Sponsorship be put on hold until the decision on the Proof of Citizenship? How can we ensure that the parent and child can travel together or stay together in Canada?
Thank you for your time and attention.
With kind regards,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
Apologies for the delay in responding to your enquiry.
A spousal sponsorship does not result in automatic urgent processing for a Proof of Citizenship application. If you are submitting a spousal sponsorship application for the parent of a child who has applied for a proof of citizenship, you should ensure that the child in question is listed on the applicant's Family Information Form (which all applicants are required to fill out, and on which all children must be listed). The form is found here: Additional Family Information [IMM 5406].
We suggest you also include a short letter of explanation indicating that an application for proof of citizenship has been submitted for a child who will be accompanying the primary applicant parent to Canada, and attach evidence of this proof application to that letter. This will provide the information that the visa officer processing the primary applicant's application needs, to look into the status of the proof application and take any necessary next steps in processing. Where appropriate, this may involve coordination with the office which is processing the proof application.
We trust this responds to your enquiry.
Regards
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Le formulaire Résidence à l'extérieur du Canada (CIT0177) s'applique uniquement aux demandeurs qui veulent compter le temps à l'extérieur du Canada pour leur calcul de la présence effective, s'ils résidaient à l’extérieur du Canada parce que:
- vous (le demandeur);
- votre époux ou conjoint de fait est citoyen canadien ou résident permanent; ou

Ces spécifications sont expliquées dans le texte "aide" à la question 9C sur le formulaire de demande CITo002 et également dans le guide d'instructions à l'étape 4 - Remplir le formulaire de demande. Cependant, nous modifierons la question afin d'offrir plus de clarté à nos candidats et à leurs représentants dès que possible. Les demandeurs peuvent répondre «non» à la question 9C s'ils ne comptent pas de temps pour des travaux du gouvernement à l'extérieur du Canada, tel que spécifié ci-dessus et n'auront pas à remplir le formulaire CIT0177. Nous apprécions que vous preniez le temps de porter cette question à notre attention et notez que cette question a été identifiée pour les futures mises à jour du formulaire CITo002. threads.subject: Common-law/Marriage-REP-2017-2313
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
The client was previously married in Pakistan and processed a divorce from his first wife, there was an error in his divorce
paperwork and his new marriage was finalized prior to his divorce effective date.
The couple have lived together in Pakistan, in a monogamous relationship since June 2015. Despite being married, would they be eligible under the common law stream.
Kind regards
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your question.
In this scenario outlined below, one person is legally married however is now living with a different partner for the past 18 months. The couple currently cohabiting may be considered common-law partners provided the marriage has broken down and they have lived separate and apart from their spouse during which time they must have cohabited in a conjugal relationship with the common-law partner for a period of at least one year. Cohabitation with a common-law partner can only be considered to have started once a physical separation from the spouse has occurred. A common-law relationship cannot be legally established if one or both parties continue to maintain a conjugal relationship with a person to whom they remain legally married.
When the sponsor is legally married to someone else, there must be sufficient evidence that there is a separation and the separated partner is no longer cohabiting with the legal spouse. The subsequent marriage that took place, while the first marriage is still legally binding, is not considered to be a legal marriage by IRCC. A common-law or conjugal partner relationship cannot be established with more than one person at the same time. Applicants must be truthful and self-identify their marital status within an application. If there is any change during the processing of the application, applicants are obliged to inform the Department of these aspects of their life change prior to the finalization of their case, including their marital status.
Applicants should provide the Statutory Declaration of Common-Law Union (IMM 5409), used in a spousal sponsorship application where the applicants are not married. A common-law couple must have lived together for at least one year, and also have intermingled financial or other affairs. In addition to submitting this form with the application, the applicants should include as many pieces of evidence to show that they are in a committed, marriage-like relationship. When information provided in the Sponsorship Evaluation and Relationship Questionnaire (IMM5532) is insufficient, an officer may request additional evidence.
For more information on documentation to prove a common-law relationship please see the following link: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=347&top=14](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=347&top=14)
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

There are changes in job duties listed in the Offer of Employment, for instance, the applicant still qualifies under the NOC code submitted in the Offer of Employment but may be working on a different project for the same employer or It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations <http://laws- lois. justice. gc. ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/page-91. html#docCont> (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209. 11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated
Cioyenneté Canada L'noaon ddmion Providing additional duties, thereby increasing weekly hours, and a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. Or, if the change in working conditions negatively impacts the worker, such as reduction in hours or salary, then a new Offer of Employment and a new work permit would be required before the change takes effect, otherwise the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer. These conditions include that an employer must:
- be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made;
- comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works;
- provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer;
- make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR. The employer cannot amend duties, hours or salary information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker. Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC. This is in response to your follow up questions regarding the eligibility to work for secondary school international students.
International students at secondary level may not work without a work permit.
International secondary school students who intend to perform work that is an essential part of their Canadian program at the secondary school level may apply for a co-op work permit. This includes vocational training programs offered by a Designated Learning Institution (DLl) in Quebec and programs that require students to work in order to obtain their secondary or high school diploma or certificate of graduation.
To avoid disruptions in student's study plans and co-op placements, IRCC encourages study permit applicants to apply for a co-op work permit at the same time as their initial study permit, if the acceptance letter provided by the DLl clearly establishes their participation in a co-op program. In that case, their co-op work permit will be issued simultaneously with their study permit, thus avoiding the additional processing delays when applying for a co-op work permit separately.
To note, applicant's acceptance letter provided by the DLl should clearly establish that the work is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. If the same program is offered without a work component, the work component cannot be considered as an essential part if the program.
The only type of work that doesn't require a work permit by the international secondary school students is volunteering. The volunteer work that the high school students will undertake fits with the "the activity is not considered to be work" description listed on the following page: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/partners-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/partners-) service-providers/educational-institutions/volunteer-work-conducted-foreign-students-when-work-permit-esdc- confirmation-required.html
